screens.title: Variables, Data Types, and Basic Operators
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we build a foundation: how programs keep data, what kinds of data Python understands, and how to work with values using operators. Think of a variable as a labeled box in memory. You give it a name, you put a value inside, and later you can read or change what’s inside. Python recognizes numbers, text, and truth values automatically so you don’t have to declare types up front. You’ll also learn the common arithmetic tools — addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, floor division, remainder, and exponentiation — plus the rules that decide which operations happen first. Finally, you’ll practice converting between types so you can avoid the common TypeError beginners see when mixing text and numbers. For example, converting a numeric string into an integer makes it usable in calculations. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to declare descriptive variable names, inspect a value’s type, use arithmetic expressions with predictable results, and perform safe conversions. That skillset is essential because nearly every program reads, stores, transforms, and outputs data; mastering these basics prevents bugs and paves the way for real calculations and user input handling. What value will you store first?

You'll also perform arithmetic using Python's operators and apply operator precedence and parentheses to produce predictable results. Finally, you will convert values between types safely to combine text and numbers without causing a TypeError. Each objective is practical: naming variables well reduces bugs, understanding types prevents invalid operations, and conversion lets you work with user input. For example, converting a numeric string to an integer makes it useful in math. We'll practice these skills with short code examples and a hands-on script so you learn how to inspect types and fix common errors. These abilities form the foundation for reading input, computing results, and producing correct output in nearly every Python program.

screens.title: How we'll practice
screens.narratorSegment: We will practice by writing a short script that declares variables of different types, prints their values and types, runs arithmetic calculations, and demonstrates converting strings to numbers. This hands-on approach shows how Python infers types and what happens when you try to mix incompatible values. You will see the specific runtime error that occurs when you try to add text and numbers together. We'll compare the incorrect version with the correct fix using explicit conversion. In addition, simple short questions will test your ability to predict results from division, floor division, and modulo operations. For example, thinking through how many full cycles fit into a total and what remainder remains will build intuition for floor division and modulo. These exercises are small and repeatable; by running them you form a mental model of how Python stores values and executes expressions. That mental model makes it easier to reason about larger programs and prevents common mistakes when combining user input and numeric computation.

screens.title: Variables and Naming Rules
screens.narratorSegment: A variable is a named storage location where a program keeps a value it can read or update later. You create a variable by assigning a value to a name with the equals operator. Names should be descriptive and follow Python naming conventions: use lowercase words separated by underscores, start with a letter or underscore, and avoid spaces or starting with a number. This naming style, called snake_case, makes your code readable to others and to future you. For example, a variable named student_age holding the number twenty makes the program self-documenting. A common beginner mistake is to use vague names like x1 or to rely on capital letters and spaces; such names reduce clarity and can also clash with built-in identifiers. Another mistake is redeclaring a variable in a way that overwrites needed data without intending to. A short concrete example: assigning the number thirty to age stores that numeric value. If you later assign a string to the same name, Python accepts it because it’s dynamically typed, but that change can lead to logic errors if other code expects a number. Takeaway: choose clear names and be deliberate when reassigning variables to avoid accidental type or logic mismatches. What descriptive variable will you use next?

Definition and rules

Key takeaway

screens.title: Dynamic Typing and Inspecting Types
screens.narratorSegment: Python is dynamically typed, which means the language infers the type of a value from what you assign rather than requiring an explicit declaration. When you store a number, Python treats it as a numeric type; when you store text in quotes, Python treats it as text. This flexibility speeds development, but it also means you must be intentional about what you store. To verify the type a value currently has, use the built-in type inspection operation. Inspecting types is especially helpful during debugging: if an expression fails, checking the runtime type often reveals the mismatch. For example, if a variable supposed to hold a numeric grade contains text because of earlier input handling, arithmetic will fail. A common misconception is to assume a string of digits behaves like a number; it does not until you convert it. Practically, you will often print a value and its type to confirm the program state. That habit prevents many errors before you write more complex logic. Now imagine receiving user input as text; converting it to a number explicitly is the safe step before calculation. Closing question: when might you prefer to leave a value as text rather than convert it to a number?

keyIdea.title: Type inspection
keyIdea.text: Python infers types dynamically. Check the current type during development to detect and fix mismatches early.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Types & Inspection
Concept
Python assigns a type to each value when you store it. During development you can inspect that type to ensure code that follows treats the value correctly. This is a lightweight debugging tool that prevents runtime errors.
Common misconception
A string of digits looks like a number but remains text until converted. Treating it as a number without conversion causes errors in arithmetic operations.
Code walkthrough
# Example script (visual only)
student_name = "Alice Smith"
student_age = 20
gpa = 3.85
is_enrolled = True

# Print values and their types
print("Name:", student_name, "Type:", type(student_name))
print("Age:", student_age, "Type:", type(student_age))
print("GPA:", gpa, "Type:", type(gpa))
print("Enrolled:", is_enrolled, "Type:", type(is_enrolled))
Running this example prints each value and the runtime classification so you can confirm the program's state.

screens.title: Integers vs Floating-Point Numbers
screens.narratorSegment: Integers represent whole numbers without decimal points. They are exact counts like zero, positive counts, or negative values. Floating-point numbers represent values with a decimal component and are used for measurements or fractional results from division. A key practical difference is how division behaves: dividing two integers with the division operator always yields a floating-point result even when the value appears whole. Another operator, floor division, discards the fractional part and returns the integer portion. This distinction matters when you need precise counts versus averaged or measured values. For example, counting students uses integers, while calculating an average grade produces a floating-point number that you may format to two decimal places for display. A common misconception is that a number that looks like an integer but has a decimal point is treated as an integer; in Python a numeric literal with a decimal is a float. When converting between these types, be mindful of precision loss: converting a float to an integer truncates the fractional part, which can be surprising if you expect rounding. Takeaway: choose int for exact counts and float for measured or fractional values, and convert explicitly when required.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Integers & Floats
Integers (int)
  • Whole numbers: 10, -5, 0.
  • Use for counts and indices.
  • Floor division returns an integer portion.
Floating-point (float)
  • Numbers with decimals: 3.14, -0.5, 2.0.
  • Results from true division are floats.
  • Converting a float to int truncates the fractional part.
Example & takeaway
If total score divided by count yields 85.666, the average is a float. If you need the number of whole completed segments, use floor division to get the integer portion. Convert explicitly and know that truncation is not rounding.

screens.title: Strings and Booleans
screens.narratorSegment: Strings hold text. You create them by surrounding characters with single or double quotes, and both forms are equivalent. Use escape sequences to include special characters inside strings, for instance a new line. Treat strings as sequences of characters when you manipulate or combine them. An important point is that strings are not numbers even if they contain only digits; to use them in math you must convert them. Booleans are the simplest type: True and False represent truth values used to make decisions. They are capitalized and commonly appear in conditions and logical expressions. A frequent beginner error is trying to concatenate a string and a number directly, which raises a type error. The safe approach is converting the number to a string before joining, or converting the text to a number when you intend to compute. Another subtle misconception is assuming that an empty string is the same as False; they are different types though in conditional expressions empty text behaves like falsey. Takeaway: manage string quoting and escapes carefully and use booleans explicitly for control flow so your program's decisions are clear.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Strings & Booleans
Strings (str)
Text inside single or double quotes. Use escape sequences to include quotes or new lines. Strings must be converted to numbers for arithmetic.
Example
Concatenate a name and a label by converting numbers to text, or format with placeholders for readability.
Booleans (bool)
Represent True or False. Used in conditions and control flow. Capitalization matters: True and False are the language values.
Practical note
An empty string is not a boolean but evaluates as falsey in condition checks; keep types explicit for clarity.

screens.title: Basic Arithmetic Operators
screens.narratorSegment: Python provides a set of arithmetic operators for computing new values from existing ones. Addition, subtraction, and multiplication behave like basic math. Division always produces a floating-point result, even when the operands are whole numbers. Floor division discards the fractional part and returns an integer portion, which is useful when you need whole counts from a division. The modulo operator returns the remainder and is handy when you want to know what is left after grouping into equal parts. Exponentiation raises a number to a power and is written as an operator for power. A concrete example: calculating an average uses true division to keep precision, while calculating how many full packages you can make from items uses floor division and modulo to report leftovers. A common error is assuming division always returns an integer; that assumption breaks logic that depends on whole number results. The practical tip is to pick the operator that matches the real-world meaning: choose floor division for whole-group counts and modulo to compute remainders. Try predicting 24 floor-divided by 7 and its modulo to build intuition.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Arithmetic
Operator list
Addition: a + b
Subtraction: a - b
Multiplication: a * b
Division (true): a / b → float
Floor division: a // b → integer portion
Modulo: a % b → remainder
Exponentiation: a ** b → power
Concrete example
If you have 24 hours and group them into 7-hour blocks, floor division gives 3 full blocks and modulo gives 3 leftover hours. Use true division to compute average scores with fractional results.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Match the operator to intent: precision versus whole-group counts and remainders.

screens.title: Operator Precedence and Grouping
screens.narratorSegment: Expressions with multiple operators follow a clear order: parentheses first, then exponentiation, followed by multiplication, division, floor division, and modulo, and finally addition and subtraction. When operators have the same precedence, evaluation proceeds left to right. This order mirrors standard arithmetic rules and prevents ambiguity. A simple but important example: adding two numbers and then multiplying versus multiplying first gives different results. Predicting the outcome becomes straightforward once you apply the precedence rules or use parentheses to force a specific grouping. A common pitfall is forgetting parentheses when combining many operations, which yields unexpected results in code used for calculations or formatting. The concrete exercise is to compute two plus three times four: without parentheses the multiplication happens first, producing fourteen; with parentheses around the sum, the result becomes twenty. Use parentheses as a readability tool and to remove any doubt about evaluation order. Final reflection: when in doubt, parenthesize the parts of an expression that represent a single logical step so your code does exactly what you intend. Operator Precedence and Grouping means remember the order: parentheses, exponentiation, multiplication/division/modulo, addition/subtraction. use parentheses to make intent explicit.. In practical terms, how python decides which operation to evaluate first. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Evaluation order
Parentheses, exponentiation, multiplication/division/floor/modulo, addition/subtraction. Left-to-right when precedence ties.
Without parentheses
2 + 3 * 4 evaluates multiplication first, producing 14. This follows standard precedence rules.
With parentheses
(2 + 3) * 4 forces addition first, producing 20. Parentheses remove ambiguity and improve readability.
Pro tip
Use parentheses to express logical grouping even when you know the precedence. This makes intent clear for reviewers and future you.

screens.title: Assignment Operators and Updating Values
screens.narratorSegment: Assignment operators let you update a variable using its current value without repeating the variable's name. The common shorthand forms include add-assign, subtract-assign, and multiply-assign among others. They are convenient and reduce duplication. For example, increasing a counter by five uses the add-assign form rather than writing the variable name twice. This makes code more concise and less error-prone when updating values repeatedly. A beginner misconception is to assume these operators create a new kind of value; they simply perform the operation on the current value and store the result back into the same name. Another important practical point is to be careful when the variable might be a non-numeric type; applying a numeric assignment operator to text will raise an error. Use explicit conversion beforehand if necessary. As an exercise, increment a score by adding points with the shorthand and then compare the expanded form to see they are equivalent. The takeaway: use assignment operators for cleaner updates, but ensure the variable's current type supports the intended operation. In practical terms, shorthand operators for common updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Shorthand forms
Add-assign: x += 5
Subtract-assign: x -= 2
Multiply-assign: x *= 3
Divide-assign: x /= 2
Equivalent expansion helps understanding: x += 5 performs x = x + 5 under the hood. Use expansion to debug unexpected results.

When tracking score, use add-assign to accumulate points. Confirm score starts numeric to avoid errors when adding.

screens.title: Type Conversion and Common TypeError Fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Type conversion, also called casting, changes the classification of a value so it can participate in a different kind of operation. The three most common conversion functions are to convert to integer, to floating-point, or to text. Use these when you need to perform numeric computation on a value that currently is text, or when you want to display a number alongside text. A very common error comes from trying to add a number and a string directly; the runtime raises a TypeError. The fix is simple: convert the number to text for concatenation or convert the text to a number for arithmetic. Be careful converting strings to numbers: if the text does not represent a valid numeric literal, the conversion raises a ValueError, so validate or handle such cases. A concrete example: a price represented as text becomes usable when transformed to a float, and quantity strings convert to integers for multiplication. In practice, confirm the string format before conversion, and prefer explicit conversions to implicit assumptions. Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Type Conversion
Common conversions
  • Convert to int when you need whole-number arithmetic.
  • Convert to float when you need decimals or precise division.
  • Convert to str when combining text with numbers for display.
Error example
Trying to add text and number directly raises a TypeError. Convert one operand to the other's type to resolve it.
Hands-on code
# Type conversion example (visual only)
price_str = "49.99"
quantity_str = "2"

# Convert and compute
price_float = float(price_str)
quantity_int = int(quantity_str)
total_cost = price_float * quantity_int

# Convert back for display
message = "Your total is: $" + str(total_cost)
print(message)
This shows converting numeric text to numbers for math, then converting the result to text for concatenation and display. Be cautious converting invalid strings which cause conversion errors.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we build a foundation: how programs keep data, what kinds of data Python understands, and how to work with values using operators. Think of a variable as a labeled box in memory. You give it a name, you put a value inside, and later you can read or change what’s inside. Python recognizes numbers, text, and truth values automatically so you don’t have to declare types up front. You’ll also learn the common arithmetic tools — addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, floor division, remainder, and exponentiation — plus the rules that decide which operations happen first. Finally, you’ll practice converting between types so you can avoid the common TypeError beginners see when mixing text and numbers. For example, converting a numeric string into an integer makes it usable in calculations. By the end of the chapter you’ll be able to declare descriptive variable names, inspect a value’s type, use arithmetic expressions with predictable results, and perform safe conversions. That skillset is essential because nearly every program reads, stores, transforms, and outputs data; mastering these basics prevents bugs and paves the way for real calculations and user input handling. What value will you store first?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to create and name variables that hold data, read back their values, and reason about what type of data is stored. You will identify integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and booleans, and explain how each type affects the operations you can perform. You'll also perform arithmetic using Python's operators and apply operator precedence and parentheses to produce predictable results. Finally, you will convert values between types safely to combine text and numbers without causing a TypeError. Each objective is practical: naming variables well reduces bugs, understanding types prevents invalid operations, and conversion lets you work with user input. For example, converting a numeric string to an integer makes it useful in math. We'll practice these skills with short code examples and a hands-on script so you learn how to inspect types and fix common errors. These abilities form the foundation for reading input, computing results, and producing correct output in nearly every Python program.

We will practice by writing a short script that declares variables of different types, prints their values and types, runs arithmetic calculations, and demonstrates converting strings to numbers. This hands-on approach shows how Python infers types and what happens when you try to mix incompatible values. You will see the specific runtime error that occurs when you try to add text and numbers together. We'll compare the incorrect version with the correct fix using explicit conversion. In addition, simple short questions will test your ability to predict results from division, floor division, and modulo operations. For example, thinking through how many full cycles fit into a total and what remainder remains will build intuition for floor division and modulo. These exercises are small and repeatable; by running them you form a mental model of how Python stores values and executes expressions. That mental model makes it easier to reason about larger programs and prevents common mistakes when combining user input and numeric computation.

A variable is a named storage location where a program keeps a value it can read or update later. You create a variable by assigning a value to a name with the equals operator. Names should be descriptive and follow Python naming conventions: use lowercase words separated by underscores, start with a letter or underscore, and avoid spaces or starting with a number. This naming style, called snake_case, makes your code readable to others and to future you. For example, a variable named student_age holding the number twenty makes the program self-documenting. A common beginner mistake is to use vague names like x1 or to rely on capital letters and spaces; such names reduce clarity and can also clash with built-in identifiers. Another mistake is redeclaring a variable in a way that overwrites needed data without intending to. A short concrete example: assigning the number thirty to age stores that numeric value. If you later assign a string to the same name, Python accepts it because it’s dynamically typed, but that change can lead to logic errors if other code expects a number. Takeaway: choose clear names and be deliberate when reassigning variables to avoid accidental type or logic mismatches. What descriptive variable will you use next?

Python is dynamically typed, which means the language infers the type of a value from what you assign rather than requiring an explicit declaration. When you store a number, Python treats it as a numeric type; when you store text in quotes, Python treats it as text. This flexibility speeds development, but it also means you must be intentional about what you store. To verify the type a value currently has, use the built-in type inspection operation. Inspecting types is especially helpful during debugging: if an expression fails, checking the runtime type often reveals the mismatch. For example, if a variable supposed to hold a numeric grade contains text because of earlier input handling, arithmetic will fail. A common misconception is to assume a string of digits behaves like a number; it does not until you convert it. Practically, you will often print a value and its type to confirm the program state. That habit prevents many errors before you write more complex logic. Now imagine receiving user input as text; converting it to a number explicitly is the safe step before calculation. Closing question: when might you prefer to leave a value as text rather than convert it to a number?

Integers represent whole numbers without decimal points. They are exact counts like zero, positive counts, or negative values. Floating-point numbers represent values with a decimal component and are used for measurements or fractional results from division. A key practical difference is how division behaves: dividing two integers with the division operator always yields a floating-point result even when the value appears whole. Another operator, floor division, discards the fractional part and returns the integer portion. This distinction matters when you need precise counts versus averaged or measured values. For example, counting students uses integers, while calculating an average grade produces a floating-point number that you may format to two decimal places for display. A common misconception is that a number that looks like an integer but has a decimal point is treated as an integer; in Python a numeric literal with a decimal is a float. When converting between these types, be mindful of precision loss: converting a float to an integer truncates the fractional part, which can be surprising if you expect rounding. Takeaway: choose int for exact counts and float for measured or fractional values, and convert explicitly when required.

Strings hold text. You create them by surrounding characters with single or double quotes, and both forms are equivalent. Use escape sequences to include special characters inside strings, for instance a new line. Treat strings as sequences of characters when you manipulate or combine them. An important point is that strings are not numbers even if they contain only digits; to use them in math you must convert them. Booleans are the simplest type: True and False represent truth values used to make decisions. They are capitalized and commonly appear in conditions and logical expressions. A frequent beginner error is trying to concatenate a string and a number directly, which raises a type error. The safe approach is converting the number to a string before joining, or converting the text to a number when you intend to compute. Another subtle misconception is assuming that an empty string is the same as False; they are different types though in conditional expressions empty text behaves like falsey. Takeaway: manage string quoting and escapes carefully and use booleans explicitly for control flow so your program's decisions are clear.

Python provides a set of arithmetic operators for computing new values from existing ones. Addition, subtraction, and multiplication behave like basic math. Division always produces a floating-point result, even when the operands are whole numbers. Floor division discards the fractional part and returns an integer portion, which is useful when you need whole counts from a division. The modulo operator returns the remainder and is handy when you want to know what is left after grouping into equal parts. Exponentiation raises a number to a power and is written as an operator for power. A concrete example: calculating an average uses true division to keep precision, while calculating how many full packages you can make from items uses floor division and modulo to report leftovers. A common error is assuming division always returns an integer; that assumption breaks logic that depends on whole number results. The practical tip is to pick the operator that matches the real-world meaning: choose floor division for whole-group counts and modulo to compute remainders. Try predicting 24 floor-divided by 7 and its modulo to build intuition.

Expressions with multiple operators follow a clear order: parentheses first, then exponentiation, followed by multiplication, division, floor division, and modulo, and finally addition and subtraction. When operators have the same precedence, evaluation proceeds left to right. This order mirrors standard arithmetic rules and prevents ambiguity. A simple but important example: adding two numbers and then multiplying versus multiplying first gives different results. Predicting the outcome becomes straightforward once you apply the precedence rules or use parentheses to force a specific grouping. A common pitfall is forgetting parentheses when combining many operations, which yields unexpected results in code used for calculations or formatting. The concrete exercise is to compute two plus three times four: without parentheses the multiplication happens first, producing fourteen; with parentheses around the sum, the result becomes twenty. Use parentheses as a readability tool and to remove any doubt about evaluation order. Final reflection: when in doubt, parenthesize the parts of an expression that represent a single logical step so your code does exactly what you intend. Assignment operators let you update a variable using its current value without repeating the variable's name. The common shorthand forms include add-assign, subtract-assign, and multiply-assign among others. They are convenient and reduce duplication. For example, increasing a counter by five uses the add-assign form rather than writing the variable name twice. This makes code more concise and less error-prone when updating values repeatedly.
